notes: \cpara{A fair translation of what Delambre, in his notice on Lagrange's life, reports Lagrange often said: Newton was ``le plus grand génie qui eût jamais existé'' and ``le plus heureux; on ne trouve qu'une fois un système du monde à établir'' (\textsc{Œuvres de Lagrange}, vol.~1, 1867).}
\cpara{Says that discovering things for oneself is more fun than reading about them, and that this is as it should be.}
\cpara{Turns to discovering what no one else knows.}

\cpara{The story of the physicist who told his girlfriend he was ``the only man in the world'' who knew why the stars shine, with the attribution hedged. In the version attributed to Houtermans, quoted in Simon Singh's \textsc{Big Bang} (2004) and cited by Wikipedia, he said: ``I've known since yesterday why it is that they shine.'' That version claims no exclusivity.}
\cpara{Says that being first to solve a major mystery is ``a tremendous high,'' ``attested by numerous sources.'' None is named.}
\cpara{States the question of the post: why should a discovery be worth less because someone else already knows the answer?}
\cpara{The first reading: after months of failed attempts, a solution that makes every piece fall into place at once.}
\cpara{Adds that the struggle yields an understanding that someone told the answer cannot get without the same study.}
\cpara{Illustrates with Maxwell.}
\cpara{The second reading: effort justification, valuing something more because it cost more, with two studies described but not cited.}

\cfact{The classic study, Aronson and Mills (1959), did not use fraternity pledges. As Wikipedia's ``Effort justification'' summarizes it, women volunteering for a discussion group on sex read embarrassing material aloud as an ``initiation,'' and those whose test was severe rated a dull group higher. I did not find a study of fraternity pledges.}

\clogic{This result does not fit the reading it illustrates. In one such study, Plassmann and colleagues (\textsc{PNAS}, 2008) told tasters different prices for the same wine, and found that ``increasing the price of a wine increases subjective reports of flavor pleasantness.'' The price was a label the tasters were told, not a cost they bore.}
\cpara{Separates the harmless case, enjoying the work for its own sake, from the less charitable one, valuing an answer more because it cost \$100.}
\cpara{An aside, offered with ``I strongly suspect'' and no evidence: much of the public's indifference to science comes from believing that free knowledge cannot be important.}
\cpara{The third reading: status, as in keeping ahead of the Joneses.}
\cpara{Does not object to competition, but notes that if the joy must come from scarcity, only one person per civilization can have it for each truth.}
\cpara{A joke on the same point: Newton used up much of the physics fun available to Earth.}
\cpara{Argues that the universe is so large that others have already made every discovery.}

\cfact{Loosely worded: the Standard Model is the theory of particle physics, and says nothing about the size of space, inflation or branching. The three claims are Max Tegmark's Levels I to III of parallel universes. In Tegmark's 2003 survey, infinite space is part of the ``cosmological concordance model,'' the second level arises ``In chaotic inflation,'' and the third holds ``In unitary quantum mechanics,'' the many-worlds reading (see the notes on ``Many Worlds, One Best Guess''); the argument that follows needs only the first.}
\cpara{Concludes, with ``may'' and a doubt about what ``before'' means, that others may have discovered gravity before Newton. On ``Tegmark duplicates,'' see the notes on ``The Bottom Line.''}
\cpara{Treats this as a reductio: if the joy requires that no one else anywhere knows, it is never available, so that requirement is ``silly.''}

\clogic{The reductio reaches only the view that the joy requires no one anywhere to know. At the scale of one civilization, the scale of the opening story and of the Nobel Prize paragraph below, other Earths change nothing. There the post's case against exclusivity is the earlier one, that it makes the joy scarce.}
\cpara{The solution: mystery is personal. If you do not know how your own hand closes, you are as ignorant as a hunter-gatherer, whoever else knows.}
\cpara{Grants that telling one's civilization something new is a real reward, one-shot per discovery, and that it can keep a researcher at a problem for years.}
\cpara{Ends by restoring ``magic and mystery'' to everything you do not personally understand, as part of the author's project to show that rationalists do not have less fun.}

\cpara{The page the post links now reads differently: ``A friend once told me that I look at the world as if I've never seen it before. But I never have seen it before! I feel like I just got here and I'm still trying to figure it out.'' I could not check the page as it stood in 2008.}
